source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock and Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models' forecasting capabilities, Study 1
finding: Gap 1. 38 single-paragraph prompts on 4 LLMs against a plain control prompt. Most prompts changed accuracy by almost nothing. After multiple-comparison correction only three helped (Frequency-Based Reasoning, Base Rate First, Step-Back) and two hurt (Bayesian Reasoning, Propose-Evaluate-Select).
numbers: 100 ForecastBench questions resolving Dec 2024, 4 models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Llama 3.1 405B), about 3,600-3,800 forecasts per model. Mean Brier GPT-4o 0.215, Haiku 0.214, Llama 0.227, Sonnet 0.208. Mixed-effects difference from control: Frequency-Based -0.014, Base Rate First -0.011, Chain of Thought -0.011, Bayesian Reasoning +0.03 (p<.001). Eight prompts beat control before correction; three after Benjamini-Hochberg. Bayesian, Propose-Evaluate-Select and Chain of Thought pushed forecasts 17-20 points from the midpoint; control only 12-13.
quote: small prompt modifications rarely boost forecasting accuracy beyond a minimal baseline
limits: Only 100 questions, one resolution month, no retrieval, single-shot prompts. The adjusted-p column in the extracted table does not match the text claim that three prompts survive correction; the text is followed here. Effects are about 0.01 Brier.
agent_relevance: Of the scaffold parts, anchoring on a base rate or frequency format and a second look (step-back) are the only prompt-level parts with support, worth about 0.01 Brier. An explicit Bayes-update instruction and propose-then-select inside one prompt hurt. Keep the schema's reference-class step; do not add a verbal Bayes procedure.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) Prompt engineering forecasting, Study 2: compound prompts, external prompts, reasoning models
finding: Gaps 1 and 5. Combining the best prompts did not stack. A prompt written by superforecasters was the only one significantly worse. Reasoning models o1 and o1-mini were no more accurate than non-reasoning models, and their mean forecasts sat below 50%, not above.
numbers: Same 100 questions, 6 models. Brier: o1-mini 0.217, o1 0.216, Llama 0.218, GPT-4o 0.208, Sonnet 0.207. Mean forecast o1 41.5% (SD 0.217) to Llama 44.8%; superforecaster Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt mean 50%; Base Rate First + Frequency-Based mean 38.4%. Base Rate First + Frequency-Based -0.004 (adj p 0.985); Base Rate First + Chain of Thought 0.0. After correction no compound prompt changed accuracy except the superforecaster Odds-Ratio prompt, which was worse.
limits: Same small question set. The question base rate is not given in the text read, so a mean of 41-45% cannot be called biased either way. Shows reasoning models do not share the 57% mean of GPT-4-era models; does not test negation pairs.
agent_relevance: Stacking human-forecaster tradecraft into one prompt gives no gain. Gains must come from outside the single prompt: retrieval, sampling, aggregation, calibration. Reasoning models are not more accurate by themselves at this scale.

source: Metaculus (2025) AI benchmark results Q3 2024 to Q1 2025: bots versus Pro forecasters
finding: Gap 2. Over three quarters, a bot team (median of the best bots) was less accurate than ten Pro forecasters on the same questions. The gap was significant overall but the quarterly trend was not resolvable. Best bots used o1 or o3-mini plus news search. A weak template bot (gpt-4o) fell from 4th to 44th as stronger bots entered.
numbers: Bot tournament 424 questions (57% binary, 21% numeric, 22% multiple choice), 34 bot makers plus 11 template bots. Pro tournament 10 Pros, 96 scorable questions. Head-to-head score -17.7, 95% CI [-28.3, -7.0], two-sided t-test p=0.0014. By quarter: Q3 2024 -11.3 [-21.8, -0.7]; Q4 2024 -8.9 [-18.8, 1]; Q1 2025 -17.7. By type: multiple choice -37.5, binary -9.8, numeric -8.7. Best bot metac-o1 (o1 + AskNews); best outside bot ManticAI (o3-mini). metac-o1 ranked 25th of 617 in the Quarterly Cup (top 5%); community prediction ranked 3rd. AskNews bots beat Exa and Perplexity bots, not significant.
limits: Read through a fetch summary of the page, not raw HTML. Early 2025 models. Bot team chosen on bot-only questions to avoid overfitting. Cup comparison only 27 questions, no significance test. Score is 100 x ln(bot/pro), not Brier.
agent_relevance: As of early 2025 the best retrieval agents were still clearly behind Pros on Metaculus questions, most of all on multiple choice. Median of bots was the team method. Later quarters not found (the aib index returned 403).

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2026) AI models have likely reached parity with superforecasters on ForecastBench
finding: Gap 2. In July 2026 the ForecastBench organisers say several submitted systems are statistically indistinguishable from the superforecaster median. The claim is parity (cannot reject equal accuracy), not clear superiority. The top systems are scaffolded multi-stage, multi-model ensembles, not plain models.
numbers: Posted 16 July 2026. One-sided bootstrap p-values vs superforecasters: Cassi AI 0.41, xAI 0.16 and 0.15, Google DeepMind 0.14. Cassi AI is the first to rank above the superforecaster median on market questions. On the preliminary dataset leaderboard 17 submissions rank above superforecasters (before: one). Preliminary results need at least 225 resolved questions. Cassi pipeline: sub-question and search-query generation, retrieval with recency filter, ensemble of several models, a second LLM analyses the reasoning to give the final forecast. Torchcast: proprietary multi-agent system.
quote: cannot reject equal forecasting accuracy at conventional significance levels
limits: Superforecaster forecasts were last collected in July 2024, so the comparison depends on a difficulty-adjusted extrapolation that the authors say grows less reliable over time. Confidence intervals overlap widely. Exact Brier values sit in image tables that could not be read. Submissions are proprietary. The leaderboard allows tools, fine-tuning and ensembling. Crowd forecasts are shown to models on market questions.
agent_relevance: Parity is plausible in 2026 only for scaffolded pipelines with search and ensembling, and the evidence is a non-rejection of equality against stale human baselines. Treat parity as unproven. A fresh superforecaster round is planned for fall 2026.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench, ICLR version: LLM ensemble baselines, aggregation, and crowd-prior prompts
finding: Gaps 4 and 9. The ForecastBench team built an LLM ensemble of 3 models x 3 superforecaster-written prompts (9 forecasts per question) and compared four aggregators. Geometric mean and geometric mean of log odds were best, median and trimmed mean slightly worse. Top LLM entries all saw the crowd forecast on market questions.
numbers: Aggregation Brier (2 SE): median 0.197 (0.024), trimmed mean 0.197 (0.024), geometric mean 0.194 (0.023), geometric mean of log odds 0.194 (0.023). Human medians: superforecasters 0.096, public 0.121, top LLM on the 200-item subset (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 0.122; with combination questions superforecasters 0.076 vs public 0.096 vs GPT-4o 0.130, a gap of 0.054. Leaderboard row: best Overall 0.123 (dataset 0.169, market 0.078, with freeze-values crowd prior) vs zero-shot Claude 3 Opus 0.134 (dataset 0.162, market 0.106).
limits: Differences between aggregators are 0.003, inside the stated error. Ensemble members were chosen on the same data (Appendix E.1). Human forecasts date from July 2024.
agent_relevance: On a fixed set, geometric mean of log odds is at least as good as any other simple pooling of 9 LLM samples and costs nothing. A crowd prior on market questions gives the largest single gain in the table, but its benefit is mostly the prior itself (see d08).

source: ForecastBench (2026) website: leaderboard definitions and human baselines
finding: Gap 2. The live site defines a Tournament board (tools, scaffolds, fine-tuning, ensembling allowed), a Baseline board (base models, no extras, run by the team) and a Preliminary board. Scores are a difficulty-adjusted Brier turned into a Brier Index (0-100%, 50% is uninformed). Overall rank is the equal-weight mean of dataset and market scores. The explore page shows a linear-trend projected parity date but gives no number in the text.
numbers: Models are added to the Tournament board 50 days after submission. Human groups were last surveyed July 2024 and answered a different question set; a two-way fixed-effects model adjusts for question difficulty. The Overall Brier Index is not the mean of the Dataset and Market indices because the transform is nonlinear.
limits: Tables and chart values are images; model names, scores and the parity date could not be read. An 'Addendum to the paper' is mentioned but was not found.
agent_relevance: Use the Baseline board for plain-model claims and the Tournament board for scaffolded systems. Never compare the two as if the condition were the same.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report (Bridgewater AIA Labs): headline results
finding: Gap 2. A multi-agent system (agentic search, 10 samples, supervisor agent, Platt scaling) scored statistically indistinguishable from the superforecaster median on ForecastBench, but trailed the market price on a harder liquid-market benchmark. Ensembling it with the market beat the market alone.
numbers: Brier, FB-Market: AIA 0.0753, superforecasters 0.0740, market 0.0965, public 0.1035. FB-7-21 (498 questions): AIA 0.1076, superforecasters 0.1110 (per-event median), public 0.1451, Karger state of the art 0.133, o3 0.1221. FB-8-14 (602 questions): AIA 0.1099, superforecasters 0.1152, public 0.1510, o3 0.1262. MarketLiquid (1,610 questions from 322 markets): AIA 0.1258, o3 0.1324, market 0.1106. Superforecaster per-event median 0.1110 beat mean 0.1123; public median 0.1450 beat mean 0.1586. Simplex-regression ensemble with market: MarketLiquid 0.106 (leave-one-out) vs market 0.111; AIA weight 0.33 [0.12, 0.47].
limits: Vendor technical report, not peer reviewed. Row labels of the o3 line in the main table are garbled in extraction. Pairwise p-value columns are row-misaligned in extraction (values 0.4328, 0.1522, 0.0946 appear to be the superforecaster-vs-AIA tests). Superforecaster data are from 2024. Platt coefficient came from outside theory, not fitted here. FB-Market is easy because of the crowd prior.
agent_relevance: Best published evidence that a scaffold can reach crowd-expert level, but it is search plus 10x sampling plus a supervisor plus calibration, i.e. many times the tokens of a plain prompt. No equal-token comparison was given.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: effect of agentic search and of showing the market price
finding: Gaps 1 and 9. Search quality matters: agentic search beat fixed three-query search, which barely beat no search. Showing the market price helps about as much as search, so the two overlap. The price alone beat the best LLM from the earlier ForecastBench paper, meaning that LLM would have done better by copying the price.
numbers: ForecastBench Brier: no search 0.1230; Search-B non-agentic 0.12168, agentic 0.11824; Search-A non-agentic 0.11738, agentic 0.1140. On the market subset: LLM no search 0.116 -> 0.103 with price (11.2% gain); best AIA config 0.085 -> 0.075 with price (11.8%). Market price alone 0.096; AIA with agentic search 0.075. Karger best LLM 0.109 on this subset vs price alone 0.096. Live markets: closed (n=64) with search 0.1002, without search 0.3609 (worse than constant 0.5 at 0.25), market 0.1111; open markets (n=1750) scored against price: 0.0522 with search, 0.0910 without.
limits: Vendor report. Search providers are anonymised. The live closed sample of 64 is too small to separate AIA from the market. Open-market score measures closeness to the price, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: A crowd or market prior helps and should be supplied when it exists, but the benefit shrinks as retrieval improves. Over-deference is shown in reverse: the earlier LLM was worse than the price it was shown. A scaffold step should test whether the final answer adds anything over the prior.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: aggregating N samples from one LLM and supervisor synthesis
finding: Gap 4. Averaging independent runs of the same agent is a strong baseline: most of the gain arrives by 5 runs, with a small extra gain to 15. Mean, trimmed mean and median are equivalent. Asking an LLM to read all the samples and write one forecast was worse than the plain mean because it over-weights outliers. A supervisor that searches to settle disagreements, and whose update is used only when it reports high confidence, gave a small further gain.
numbers: FB-7-21, 10 forecasts: simple mean 0.1140, trimmed mean 0.1142, median 0.1138, single forecast 0.1182. Supervisors: agentic 0.1125 (top-3 rate 33.9%), non-agentic (Halawi-style) 0.1168, best-of-k 0.1191, none 0.1199. MarketLiquid Brier fell sharply from 1 to 5 forecasts and modestly to 15 (bootstrap from 50 forecasts per question). Authors adopt 10.
limits: The 'none' baseline (0.1199) differs from the simple mean (0.1140) on the same benchmark, so baselines differ between tables. Gains of 0.002-0.006 are small. No comparison of one-model sampling with mixed-model crowds at equal tokens; the ForecastBench ensemble (d05) used mixed models but no single-model arm.
agent_relevance: Use the mean (or logit mean) of about 5-10 independent samples; do not let a model re-read samples and pick. A disagreement-resolution step with fresh search is the only synthesis that helped. Equal-token comparison of single-model sampling versus mixed-model crowds is untested.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Platt scaling and log-odds extremization on LLM forecasts, with out-of-distribution fit
finding: Gap 3. LLM forecasts hedge toward 0.5. Post-hoc extremizing helps. Log-odds extremization with a fixed multiplier and Platt scaling are mathematically the same on the geometric mean. A parameter fitted on a different benchmark transfers but loses part of the gain. The authors say it only helps when the forecast is already on the right side of 0.5.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier: none 0.1140; log-odds extremization fixed d=3 0.1085; Platt scaling with fixed parameter 0.1076. Learned-parameter rows (as printed, mapping uncertain): Platt ID leave-one-out 0.1071, OOD (fit on Halawi 2024 set) 0.1104; OLS 0.1097 ID / 0.1134 OOD; none 0.1119 ID / 0.1125 OOD; isotonic regression 0.1097. Fixed value equals a Platt coefficient of about 1.73 (root of 3, from Neyman and Roughgarden 2022). Optimal coefficient for superforecasters 1.72; for AIA 2.27. AIA beat superforecasters at every coefficient tried. Largest gains in forecasts of 0.2-0.4 and 0.6-0.8; a move 0.497 to 0.381 changes Brier by -0.102; 0.995 to 0.999 by 2.4e-5.
limits: Table 11 is hard to read after extraction, so the row-to-column mapping of ID/OOD numbers is uncertain. One benchmark. Mandel-Barnes a=2.2 (human analysts) and the AIA optimum 2.27 are of similar size but use different parameterisations; do not equate them.
agent_relevance: Apply a mild post-hoc log-odds stretch to the pooled forecast (fixed coefficient near 1.7 to 2.3), never to a single sample, and only after the direction of the call is trusted. A fixed theory value is safer than a fitted one. Re-fit on resolved questions as they arrive.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: foreknowledge (date leak) checks and model comparison
finding: Gap 8. Leakage in search is measurable and fixable. The authors audit 502 search traces, estimate 1.65% of results leak the outcome, and show scores barely move when flagged questions are removed. But one model (gpt-oss-120b) looked best only because it exploited leaks. Live-market testing avoids the problem.
numbers: Judge audit n=502: 16 true positives, 65 false positives, 412 true negatives, 9 false negatives. ForecastBench Brier: baseline 0.1159, filtered 0.1161 (+0.17%), worst case (flagged set to 0.5) 0.1166 (+0.55%). MarketLiquid base models (no supervisor): GPT-4o 0.1485, Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.1456, GPT-5 0.1412, Qwen-32b 0.1404, o3 0.1242, Claude Sonnet 4 0.1195. gpt-oss-120b 0.1076 was a mirage: 17.09% of its queries leaked, touching 57% of the benchmark. Sonnet 4's reliable cutoff (Jan 2025) overlaps the benchmark start, so its number may include lookahead.
limits: Own audit by the vendor. Leak rate depends on search provider and query style. Model rankings differ by benchmark.
agent_relevance: Cleanest set-ups are live forward-resolving questions (d03, d04, d12) and pastcasting with frozen retrieval. Any agent comparison must log which documents it saw and check their dates.

source: Yang et al. (2025) LLM-as-a-Prophet: Prophet Arena
finding: Gaps 2, 5 and 10. On 1,367 resolved Kalshi events, frontier reasoning models scored about the same Brier as the market baseline and were better calibrated, yet most lost money against the market. The models pass logical-consistency and prompt-robustness sanity checks.
numbers: Brier (95% CI): GPT-5 0.184 (0.006), Grok-4 0.189, Claude Sonnet 4 0.194, Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.197, Llama-4-Scout 0.219, market baseline 0.187. ECE about 0.04 for the strong models vs 0.067-0.069 for the market (as printed). Average return of the top model (GPT-5) 0.943, below break-even at 1. All LLM Briers fall in [0.18, 0.22]. Sample is 76% sports, 8% entertainment, 7% politics, 9% other. The stronger model was best in the extreme bins (0-0.1 and 0.9-1.0).
limits: Event mix is mostly sports, unlike geopolitics. Everyone gets the same fixed news context, so retrieval is not tested. Section 4 analyses use a 100-event subset. The consistency claim ('largely mature') is a summary; details are in appendices not read.
agent_relevance: On a clean live set, frontier models in late 2025 are near market-level Brier but not above it. Calibration is already fair for the strongest models, so post-hoc stretching probably helps less for them than for older models.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) FutureX: a live benchmark for LLM agents in future prediction
finding: Gap 2. A daily-updated live benchmark of 25 models and agents. Reasoning models with search beat the rest. The top systems still trail professional sell-side analysts on earnings forecasts.
numbers: Overall score weights 10/20/30/40% for Levels 1-4. Grok-4 best overall, then Gemini-2.5-flash Deep Research, GPT-o4-mini Think&Search, Seed1.6. Analyst case study (S&P 500, Q2 2025): best models beat the sell-side consensus on 37.5% of revenue and 32.3% of EPS forecasts; Gemini-2.5-pro average win rate 33.0% (revenue) and 33.7% (EPS); no model passes 50%.
limits: Scores are accuracy or F1 style, not Brier, so it does not test probability calibration. Questions are open-ended facts that resolve soon. Finance only for the analyst comparison.
agent_relevance: Search plus reasoning matters more than raw model size on live prediction. Supports retrieval as the main lever. Says little about probability quality.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: what works, what fails? Judgment and Decision Making 13(6)
finding: Gaps 3 and 7. A different agency (UK analysts, not the Canadian unit). A structured method (ACH) did not improve probability accuracy. Statistical repair did: forcing judgments to sum to one, then averaging analysts, cut error by 61%. Equal-weighted averaging beat coherence-weighted averaging. This is an extension, not a replication of the Canadian forecast-skill result.
numbers: 50 UK analysts (ACH n=25, control n=25), mean age 27.79, mean experience 14.08 months. Raw MAE ACH 0.26 vs control 0.21 (p=.14, d=0.43). Mean sum of four probabilities 1.77 vs 1.54 (should be 1). Coherentization cut MAE 0.23 to 0.15 (35%, d=0.96); simple normalisation 0.13. Averaging all 50 coherentized judgments gave MAE 0.09 (61% below 0.23). Extremizing was not tested.
limits: Hypothetical scenario with a Bayesian answer key, not real-world forecasts. Small, junior sample. Much of the aggregation gain is variance reduction (random responses improve similarly).
agent_relevance: Evidence that coherence repair and plain averaging work for noisy judges, and that a method like ACH needs a test. The agent should normalise hypothesis probabilities to sum to one before use.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2018) Geopolitical forecasting skill in strategic intelligence, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making
finding: Gap 7. Same authors, same organisation, larger sample: the 2014 result held up. This is the closest thing to a replication found, and it is internal. High discrimination and good calibration with underconfidence remained. Skill was not just from easy questions.
numbers: 3,622 forecasts extracted from strategic intelligence reports; codable subset N=2,013 (verbal probabilities mapped to numbers); 1,609 uncodable. Forecasts with p<=0.05 or >=0.95 discriminated worse than those in between, and calibration did not differ. If all 1,609 uncodable forecasts were set to 0.5 (cautious ignorance), skill remained a large improvement over guessing strategies.
limits: Abstract only read (via Crossref); the full text is paywalled (403). Same Canadian unit, so not independent. No replication in another agency or country was found.
agent_relevance: Verbal-to-numeric mapping was needed and 44% of forecasts could not be coded, so vague language itself lowers usability. The agent should output numbers or fixed-scale phrases, never free prose.

source: Mandel and Irwin (2021) Facilitating sender-receiver agreement in communicated probabilities: words, numbers or both? Judgment and Decision Making
finding: Gap 6. Numeric and combined verbal+numeric formats agreed with a bounded scale better than words alone. Words alone were worse at telling low from high probability and showed the fifty-fifty blip. Adding words to numbers gave no gain.
numbers: N=1,202 participants, three agreement measures; numeric and combined formats beat verbal on all three.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref). Tests receivers' reading of a standard scale, not forecast accuracy of words versus numbers.
agent_relevance: Do not make the agent hedge with Kent-scale words. Ask for numbers (optionally with the word beside them) and score the numbers.

source: Belem, Kelly, Steyvers, Singh and Smyth (2024) Perceptions of linguistic uncertainty by language models and humans
finding: Gap 6. LLMs mostly map phrases like 'probably' and 'highly unlikely' to numbers as people do, but their mapping shifts with what the model believes about the statement. This is about reading others' words, not about the model's own verbal forecasts.
numbers: 14 expressions, 10 LLMs. Larger or newer models (GPT-4, Llama3 70B, Gemini) reach 85% or more agreement with the human modal values (PA score); 7 of 10 LLMs match the population mode better than individual humans do. Prior-knowledge bias: all 10 LLMs lose PA on verifiable statements, an average drop of 4.3 points vs 0.9 for humans; mean answers about 7.0 points higher for true than false statements; for 'possible' the true-false gap is 49.5 points vs about 5.7 for 'uncertain'.
limits: Studies third-party statements, not an LLM's own forecasts. No accuracy measure against outcomes. 2024-generation models.
agent_relevance: No study was found that scores LLM verbal forecasts against outcomes. If the agent must use words, map them with a fixed table and avoid 'possible'. Prefer numbers from the start.

source: Baron, Mellers, Tetlock, Stone and Ungar (2014) Two reasons to make aggregated probability forecasts more extreme, Decision Analysis (abstract opened)
finding: Gap 3. Two separate reasons to stretch a pooled forecast: averaging noisy probabilities pulls the result toward 0.5 (not so for the median or mean log odds), and forecasters ignore that others hold different information. One transformation with different parameters handles both.
numbers: Abstract only: no parameter values were read this session. Earlier note a28 stays unopened for numbers.
limits: Parameter values not verified. Human GJP data, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Median or log-odds mean remove the first distortion for free; the second needs a stretch. For one LLM sampled many times the second reason may not apply, since all samples share one body of information. This is untested.

source: Neyman and Roughgarden (2022) Are you smarter than a random expert? The robust aggregation of substitutable signals
finding: Gap 3. Theory: when experts' information has diminishing returns, averaging beats a random expert, and if the prior is known, averaging then extremizing by a constant factor gives strong guarantees. This is the source of the fixed value d=3 that AIA uses.
numbers: Abstract: extremizing means moving the average away from the prior by a constant factor. See d10 for its use (d=3, Platt coefficient about 1.73).
limits: Abstract only read. The guarantee depends on the 'projective substitutes' condition, untested on LLM samples.
agent_relevance: Gives a defensible fixed multiplier. It is a modelling assumption, not a measured LLM fact.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2026) Can you judge a forecast by its rationale?
finding: Gap 10. A label-free proxy for human forecast quality works moderately well. GPT-4o scored each rationale on 60 quality markers; the combined score correlated with accuracy, more at the forecaster level than the single-forecast level. Low scores warn more than high scores praise.
numbers: ACE tournament 2011-2015, over 55,000 forecast-rationale pairs, about $0.007 each (about $400). Composite vs accuracy: forecast level r=.19 (pre-LLM benchmark .06), forecaster level r=.51 (benchmark .39). Rationale length vs human rating r=.62 but unrelated to accuracy. Bottom third of scores: accuracy +0.09; middle and top thirds +0.01 and +0.02. Positive markers: forecast and rationale align, fact based, concrete reasoning. Negative: gut based, confirmation bias, extreme confidence.
limits: Blog post on a working paper; not peer reviewed. Correlational. Human rationales, not agent traces. LLM scoring accuracy against human coders not reported.
agent_relevance: A rubric check of the agent's own rationale (facts cited, forecast matches reasoning) is a cheap label-free signal at the single-forecast level, but only r near .2. Use it to flag the worst forecasts, not to rank good ones.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2026) Can we identify better and worse forecasters using easy-to-resolve questions?
finding: Gap 10. Quick calibration questions answered before forecasting had a modest link to later accuracy on a hard, slow-resolving question.
numbers: 77 forecasters (superforecasters, biosecurity and virology experts), 9 usable calibration questions. Correlation r=0.267 between calibration rank and score on the RCT forecast. Top 15 by calibration beat 99 of 100 random groups of 15; bottom 15 were worse than all 100.
limits: Single study; top/bottom 15 cut-off chosen after the fact. An intersubjective proxy was weaker, with no number given.
agent_relevance: Weak support for cheap proxy checks. For an LLM, held-out consistency checks (K07) still failed to generalise; nothing here shows that proxies survive optimisation.

source: Mandel et al. (2024) The effect of calibration training on the calibration of intelligence analysts' judgments, Applied Cognitive Psychology
finding: Gaps 3 and 7. Another group of analysts: calibration training moved bias toward less confidence rather than improving monitoring. Overconfident on interval questions before training, underconfident on binary questions, and training made the binary underconfidence worse.
numbers: 70 intelligence analysts, before-after design with interval estimation and binary choice tasks. Gains on the two tasks were uncorrelated.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref). Almanac-style tasks, not real forecasts.
agent_relevance: Fits the pattern in Mandel-Barnes: analysts underconfident on binary calls. Post-hoc stretching can repair a lean; training only moves the lean. Prefer fixed transforms to instructions to 'be more confident'.

source: Chandak, Goel, Prabhu, Hardt and Geiping (2026) Scaling open-ended reasoning to predict the future (OpenForecaster)
finding: Gap 3. Training an 8B model on automatically built open-ended forecasting questions, with an accuracy-plus-Brier reward, matched much larger proprietary models. Rewarding accuracy alone damaged calibration; Brier alone helped less on accuracy. The calibration gain carried over to SimpleQA, GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro.
numbers: Held-out test May-August 2025. Accuracy-only reward gave negative Brier scores, worse than a constant. Accuracy+Brier reward best on both. Qwen3 thinking models; compared with gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek-R1, Grok-3-mini.
limits: Open-ended questions, not binary probability forecasts. Training, not a scaffold. Numeric figures are in charts that could not be read.
agent_relevance: Calibration can be learned and transfers, which a scaffold cannot do. For a scaffold-only agent, keep a post-hoc calibration map.
